A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CORE compression framework despite the changed title. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original QA accuracy and compression results, training-stage ablations, compressor comparisons, downstream-model transfer experiments, and case studies.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds LongBench evaluation, cross-dataset transfer, noisy-context experiments, and additional baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: Both versions use DeepSeek-V3 distillation with the same filtering rules, followed by GRPO optimization using EM plus weighted F1 rewards and a frozen downstream LLM. Greedy decoding is newly documented, while the open-ended-task discussion proposes possible extensions without establishing an implemented method change.

E1.justification: v4 adds LongBench evaluation on MuSiQue and long-context variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA (Appendix D.1). Their context lengths and document construction differ from the retained retrieval benchmarks. It also adds NQ evaluation with shuffled irrelevant passages. These substantially extend the represented inputs and test environments.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated LongLLMLingua and QGC baselines to both the five-document and ten-document comparisons in Table 1, materially broadening the principal compression comparison. Existing comparators remain, and the corresponding downstream-LLM transfer and alternative-compressor tables retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on NQ and evaluating on HotpotQA, evaluating LongBench using HotpotQA-trained compressors with F1 and token counts, and constructing noisy NQ inputs from three DPR passages plus seven random Wikipedia passages followed by shuffling. The original benchmark splits, retrieval setup, model configurations, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.7 adds cross-dataset transfer analysis, and Appendix D.2 tests resistance to irrelevant, shuffled context without noise-augmented training. Figure 4 adds F1 sensitivity curves alongside the existing EM analysis. The original stage ablations, compressor-size comparisons, downstream-LLM transfer analysis, and two case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained five GRPO rollouts per sample describe training, not repeated experimental evaluations.

E6.justification: Shared table values and case-study outputs are unchanged. v4 adds baseline scores, F1 sensitivity curves, LongBench results, cross-dataset transfer results, and noisy-NQ results. For example, CORE/full-context scores are 38.94/38.41 F1 on LongBench MuSiQue and 38.19/35.21 EM on noisy NQ. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over matched v3 results. The prose changes the five-document EM-gain range from 1–7 to 1.5–6.9, although unchanged Table 1 implies 0.68–7.08.

T1.justification: Equation 1 expands the previously stated cross-entropy loss into token-level log probabilities, and Equation 2 introduces shorthand for the existing probability ratio. The filtering conditions, GRPO objective, and reward definitions are mathematically retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that a lightweight compressor optimized using downstream task feedback preserves or improves QA accuracy while greatly reducing context, retaining the headline 3% compression ratio and 3.3-point average EM gain. v4 foregrounds the existing distillation stage and changes the title without materially changing the central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands applicability and efficiency discussion: Section 3.4 proposes task-specific rewards for generation, summarization, and dialogue, while Appendix B develops training, inference, and retraining-cost arguments. Section 4.7 qualifies cross-dataset transfer as nearly lossless despite degradation relative to target-dataset training. The alpha discussion also narrows improvement to the majority of cases. Open-ended applicability remains proposed rather than experimentally demonstrated.

D1.justification: v4 replaces the promised code release with a repository URL and newly specifies greedy decoding, validation-based alpha selection over 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0, and approximately five hours of RL training on eight H20 GPUs. Most implementation settings are retained or relocated. Conversely, Figure 3 replaces v3's explicit few-shot QA examples with an Examples placeholder, reducing prompt specificity.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to discuss soft compression, including xRAG, and prompt compression methods including LongLLMLingua, DAC, and TACO-RL. It develops new distinctions between generative compression and token deletion, and between training a fixed-generator compressor and training the generator itself. Earlier citations to RA-DIT, REPLUG, and RAFE are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before methodology, experiments and appendices are reorganized, and inference receives a dedicated subsection. The title, author information, and disclosures also change. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v4 changes the document from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Figures are redrawn or relocated, the two appendix prompt figures are merged into main-text Figure 3, and Figure 4 gains an F1 panel. Table 1 gains baseline rows and shaded groups, and three new experimental tables are added.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important gaps in v3's evidence by extending five- and ten-document evaluations to much longer LongBench contexts, injected retrieval noise, and cross-dataset transfer, including a documented transfer limitation. Additional relevant baselines and implementation disclosures strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit few-shot examples and the inaccurate revised EM-gain summary. Statistical uncertainty and measured inference-latency comparisons remain absent, but the empirical support for applicability and robustness is substantially stronger.
